reading.title: Same Letters, Fresh Meanings
reading.purpose: See how one spelled word can change its meaning and even its stress from sentence to sentence.
paras: Some English words are like actors who wear two costumes. They keep the exact same spelling, yet their meaning changes depending on the sentence.

Look at words from math and science. A figure can be a written number like 42, or the outline of a statue. Volume can mean how loud a radio plays, or the space inside a water jug. A degree measures temperature on a thermometer, and it also names a title earned after college. When farmers plant corn, healthy soil will yield a big harvest; on a street corner, drivers yield to let walkers cross first.

Other words even shift which syllable you stress! A bakery can produce warm loaves, while a grocer stacks fresh produce like apples and greens. You can record a song on a phone, or break a school track record. You can present a poster in class, or wrap a birthday present.

Listen for the shift in these last three pairs too. A citizen may object to an unfair rule, while a shiny rock is an object on a shelf. A jar's content is what sits inside it, yet a cozy cat feels content and happy. Finally, scientists conduct careful tests, and teachers praise polite conduct in the hall.
When you read aloud, context tells you both what the word means and how to say it.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, what are two meanings of the word "yield"?
choices: to give a crop harvest and to let walkers go first
to measure temperature and to earn a college title after school
to wrap a birthday gift and to show a class poster
to save a song on a phone and to win a track race
qs.why: Paragraph 2 says healthy soil will yield a big harvest, and drivers yield to let walkers cross first.

qs.q: Which sentence shows two different meanings of the word "content"?
choices: Listen for the shift in these last three pairs too.
A citizen may object to an unfair rule, while a shiny rock is an object on a shelf.
A jar's content is what sits inside it, yet a cozy cat feels content and happy.
When you read aloud, context tells you both what the word means and how to say it.
qs.why: This sentence contrasts what sits inside a jar with a cat feeling happy and satisfied.

ev.text: A jar's content is what sits inside it, yet a cozy cat feels content and happy.

qs.q: At the farmers' market, Maya bought carrots, pears, and spinach. Which word from the reading names these fresh foods?
qs.why: Paragraph 3 explains that a grocer stacks fresh produce like apples and greens.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Bakers and grocers use more tricky vocabulary words than scientists or teachers do.
Some words keep one spelling while changing meaning and sound based on context.
Every English word with two syllables changes its meaning when you read it aloud.
Drivers and farmers should always use different words so nobody gets confused.
qs.why: The reading shows multiple examples of words with one spelling and two or more meanings, guided by context.

clues.text: how loud a radio plays, or the space inside a water jug
